name: Peony
fact: In China the peony is called the "king of flowers," a symbol of honor and wealth — and some plants live over 100 years.

name: Sacred Lotus
fact: Lotus seeds can stay alive for over a thousand years — one sprouted from a ~1,300-year-old seed. Its leaves are also self-cleaning.

name: Cherry Blossom
fact: Japan's cherry blossoms bloom for only about one to two weeks, and the tradition of hanami (flower viewing) is over a thousand years old.

name: Sunflower
fact: Young sunflowers track the sun across the sky, turning from east to west during the day and resetting overnight.

name: Tulip
fact: During the Dutch "tulip mania" of the 1630s, a single rare bulb could sell for more than the price of a house.

name: Orchid
fact: Vanilla flavoring comes from the seed pod of a climbing orchid — the only orchid grown for food.

name: Rose
fact: Roses have been cultivated for around 5,000 years, and fossilized roses date back some 35 million years.

name: Lavender
fact: Its name comes from the Latin "lavare," to wash — the Romans used lavender to scent their baths.

name: Calla Lily
fact: Despite the name it isn't a true lily — the showy "flower" is actually a curved modified leaf called a spathe.

name: Bird of Paradise
fact: Named for its resemblance to a tropical bird, it's pollinated by sunbirds that perch on it to sip nectar.

name: Hydrangea
fact: Its color depends on the soil: acidic soil turns the blooms blue, while alkaline soil turns them pink.

name: Snapdragon
fact: When the flower fades, its dried seed pod looks eerily like a tiny human skull.

name: Foxglove
fact: The heart medicine digitalis comes from foxglove — though the plant itself is quite poisonous.

name: Marigold
fact: Marigolds are central to Mexico's Day of the Dead, where their scent is believed to guide spirits home.

name: Chrysanthemum
fact: In Japan the chrysanthemum symbolizes the Emperor — the imperial seat is even called the Chrysanthemum Throne.

name: Poppy
fact: The red field poppy became a worldwide symbol of remembrance for fallen soldiers after World War I.

name: Lily of the Valley
fact: Sweetly fragrant but very poisonous, it has appeared in the wedding bouquets of several royal brides.

name: Iris
fact: Named after the Greek goddess of the rainbow; the heraldic fleur-de-lis is a stylized iris.

name: Dahlia
fact: The national flower of Mexico, the dahlia comes in thousands of varieties and nearly every color except true blue.

name: Camellia
fact: Tea comes from a camellia (Camellia sinensis), and camellia shrubs can live for hundreds of years.

name: Magnolia
fact: Magnolias are ancient — they evolved before bees existed, so they're pollinated by beetles instead.

name: Wisteria
fact: Wisteria vines can live over a century; the largest, in Sierra Madre, California, covers about an acre.

name: Jasmine
fact: Many jasmines release their perfume at night to attract moths, and it's the national flower of several countries.

name: Hibiscus
fact: In the tropics, hibiscus flowers are brewed into a tart, ruby-red tea rich in vitamin C.

name: Forget-Me-Not
fact: Tied to a medieval legend of lost love, it's now a symbol of remembrance and Alzheimer's awareness.

name: Bleeding Heart
fact: Its arching stems dangle rows of pink, heart-shaped blooms, each with a little white "drop" beneath.

name: Ranunculus
fact: Also called the Persian buttercup, its tightly layered petals make it look like a delicate paper rose.

name: Anemone
fact: Its nickname is "windflower," from the Greek — the petals open and close with the light and breeze.

name: King Protea
fact: South Africa's national flower is named after Proteus, the shape-shifting Greek god, for its many forms.

name: Cosmos
fact: Its name comes from the Greek "kosmos," meaning harmony, for the neat, even spacing of its petals.

name: Freesia
fact: Prized in perfumery, freesia has a sweet, slightly peppery scent that's hard to reproduce artificially.

name: Gardenia
fact: Intensely fragrant, gardenia petals bruise and turn yellow at the lightest touch.

name: Sweet Pea
fact: Grown purely for its fragrance rather than food — despite the name, its seeds are actually toxic.

name: Delphinium
fact: Its name comes from the Greek for "dolphin," which the flower's bud was thought to resemble.

name: Columbine
fact: The name comes from the Latin for "dove" — the spurred petals look like a ring of doves.

name: Cornflower
fact: Once a common weed in grain fields, its vivid blue was used for dye and it's a traditional symbol in Germany.

name: Daffodil
fact: The birth flower of March and a herald of spring; every part is toxic, which is why deer leave it alone.

name: Saffron Crocus
fact: Saffron, the world's most expensive spice, is hand-picked from this crocus — it takes ~150 flowers per gram.

name: Hyacinth
fact: Named after a youth in Greek myth, this spring bulb is famous for its powerful, sweet fragrance.

name: Pansy
fact: Its name comes from the French "pensée," meaning thought — the face-like bloom stands for remembrance.

name: Zinnia
fact: In 2016 a zinnia became one of the first flowers ever grown and bloomed aboard the International Space Station.

name: Water Lily
fact: Claude Monet painted around 250 canvases of the water lilies in his garden pond at Giverny.

name: Bougainvillea
fact: The vivid "petals" are actually colorful bracts — the real flower is the tiny white bloom at the center.

name: Plumeria
fact: Used to make Hawaiian leis, plumeria has no nectar — it tricks moths into pollinating it with scent alone.

name: Lilac
fact: A beloved sign of spring, the fragrant lilac actually belongs to the same family as the olive tree.

name: Aster
fact: Named from the Greek word for "star" after its shape, the aster is a symbol of love and patience.

name: Gerbera Daisy
fact: Cheerful and bold, the gerbera is one of the most popular cut flowers in the world.

name: Carnation
fact: One of the oldest cultivated flowers — grown for over 2,000 years — and the traditional flower of Mother's Day.

name: Morning Glory
fact: Its blooms open at dawn and fade by afternoon; cultivating "asagao" is a centuries-old art in Japan.

name: Edelweiss
fact: Growing high in the Alps, its white woolly hairs shield it from cold and UV — a symbol of rugged devotion.
